# Owner interaction preferences

Personal preferences from the repo owner for how the assistant should interact — tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, how results and decisions are surfaced, and the phrases the owner uses to trigger defined commands. These are **not** project conventions (those live in the [packs/](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/tree/main/packs) corpus, each pack bundling its skills); they're how the owner likes to be worked with. Where a preference triggers a command whose mechanics are a project convention, the mechanics stay in their own doc and the entry here just owns the trigger phrase.

## Preferences

- **End every turn with a blockquote callout** — `> ✅ All done`, or `> ⚠️ Still open: …` listing what remains — never hedged in prose.
- **"LGTM"** merges the change at hand into `main` (`merge-to-main` skill); it approves that change only, never later work.
- **"bump version"** raises the project's version; the project's own workflow decides how it changes and which files change.
- **In the conversation**: link every source-controlled document you edit, display every image you edit, link every issue/PR number.
- **Ask every decision or approval through an `AskUserQuestion` popup, never prose** — one question per item, each with its case.
- **Enclose anything the owner will lift elsewhere** — a prompt, a message, copy to paste — in one delimited block, boundaries unmistakable.
- **Prefix a prompt for another session, inside its block, with a disclaimer**: Claude wrote it — examine inconsistencies, don't follow blindly.
- **Open a pull request right after committing to a branch**, unasked — overriding Claude Code's default of waiting to be told.
- **Keep working through a multi-step plan without pausing for approval of each step** — aggregate the steps into one substantial change to review, and stop only for an action that reaches the world (a release, a fleet-wide effect, anything irreversible) or a decision only the owner can make.

## github
The GitHub MCP Server provides tools to interact with GitHub platform.

Tool selection guidance:
	1. Use 'list_*' tools for broad, simple retrieval and pagination of all items of a type (e.g., all issues, all PRs, all branches) with basic filtering.
	2. Use 'search_*' tools for targeted queries with specific criteria, keywords, or complex filters (e.g., issues with certain text, PRs by author, code containing functions).

Context management:
	1. Use pagination whenever possible with batches of 5-10 items.
	2. Use minimal_output parameter set to true if the full information is not needed to accomplish a task.

Tool usage guidance:
	1. For 'search_*' tools: Use separate 'sort' and 'order' parameters if available for sorting results - do not include 'sort:' syntax in query strings. Query strings should contain only search criteria (e.g., 'org:google language:python'), not sorting instructions. Always call 'get_me' first to understand current user permissions and context. ## Issues

Check 'list_issue_types' first for organizations to use proper issue types. Use 'search_issues' before creating new issues to avoid duplicates. Always set 'state_reason' when closing issues. ## Pull Requests

PR review workflow: Always use 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'create' to create a pending review, then 'add_comment_to_pending_review' to add comments, and finally 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'submit_pending' to submit the review for complex reviews with line-specific comments.

Before creating a pull request, search for pull request templates in the repository. Template files are called pull_request_template.md or they're located in '.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE' directory. Use the template content to structure the PR description and then call create_pull_request tool.

- session-start-hook: Creating and developing startup hooks for Claude Code on the web. Use when the user wants to set up a repository for Claude Code on the web, create a SessionStart hook to ensure their project can run tests and linters during web sessions.
- adopt-claudinite: Bootstrap Claudinite into a consuming repo — mount, hooks, checks, skills. Use when asked to bootstrap, adopt, or set up Claudinite, or to baseline a repo to pick up updates.
- adopt-pack: Add one or more packs to an already-adopted Claudinite member — declare, run each pack's adoption interview, re-vendor, scaffold, land. Use when asked to adopt, add, enable, or declare a pack (e.g. product-wiki, executable-requirements) on a repo that already runs Claudinite.
- authoring-agent-docs: How to write instruction files coding agents follow reliably. Use before writing or editing any Claude instruction doc — a project CLAUDE.md, a convention doc, a routine spec.
- bug-investigation: Method for investigating a bug and pinning down its root cause. Use when investigating a bug report, when a fix didn't hold or a bug recurs, or when a report doesn't reproduce against main.
- bump-version: Raise the project's version — a minor bump by default. Use when the owner says "bump version".
- ci-performance-evaluation: Method for finding where a repo's CI time actually goes and what is worth fixing. Use when CI feels slow, when investigating a runtime regression, or when the weekly ci-performance task hands you a finding.
- extract-from-activity: Mine a window of a repo's commits, merged PRs and issue activity for durable, reusable lessons and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from repo artifacts — the growth-extract task's activity half, or an owner asking what a recent stretch of work taught.
- extract-from-conversations: Mine an agent-user conversation — a captured conversation log or the live session — for friction-driven lessons (misunderstandings, backtracks, measured wall-time waits) and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from a session transcript or the conversation-logs branch, or when an owner asks for a retrospective.
- file-placement: Where a file should live — the reference-distance metric, the high-reach code smell, and the mandated-location, test-location and plugin-contract exemptions. Use before placing, moving, or renaming a file, or when reviewing where one lives.
- generate-project-instructions: Decompose a project into its pack facets (working-style class, technology, aspect, domain) and extract its working instructions into reusable canon packs plus the project's own local packs (.claudinite/local_packs/). Use when a project has no established working style yet, or it exhibits a facet no pack covers — during bootstrap of a fresh/empty repo, or on an uplevel request.
- github-actions-scheduling: What a GitHub Actions `schedule:` trigger actually guarantees — late fires, dropped fires, the 60-day disable — and how to build and describe scheduled work around it. Use when adding, changing, explaining, or debugging anything that runs on a cron in GitHub Actions.
- growth-dedup: Prune a repo's local packs of items the mounted Claudinite canon now covers — remove, strip to residue, or track a wording drift, never grow an entry. Use when the growth dedup task runs, or when asked to reconcile or dedup local packs against the canon.
- prose-to-checks: Mine pack prose (RULES.md, SKILL.md) for always-testable rules that were never converted to checks, and convert the strongest ones. Use when auditing packs for convertible rules, when the weekly prose-to-checks sweep runs, or as the upgrade pass over prose a growth-extract run just wrote.
- repo-text-sweeps: Mechanics for grep/sed sweeps, renames, and path relocations across a repo. Use before a bulk find-replace, a rename, or moving files — and after one, to catch silently broken references.
- single-branch-status: Assess one branch's landed status — merged, already-in-main, superseded, orphaned, or genuine unmerged work — read-only. Use when triaging whether a single branch is safe to delete, judging by content not the ref's name (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-branches task hands you branches to assess).
- single-issue-triage: Triage one open issue and take the first applicable action — close-if-implemented, needs-decision, blocked, quick-win, or leave. Use when acting on a single issue; "implemented in main" must be verified against main's current content and the default is to comment, not close (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-issues task hands you issues to triage).
- single-pr-status: Assess one open pull request's landed status — keep-open, or closeable (merged, already-in-main, superseded, stale) — read-only. Use when triaging whether a single PR should stay open, judging by its commits and diff not its title (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-prs task hands you PRs to assess).
- unattended-agents: Architecture and practices for unattended, automation-invoked agents and recurring routines. Use when building, structuring, or running an AI agent, a scheduled routine, or a multi-stage agent pipeline.
- writing-claudinite-skills: Authoring or changing a skill in the Claudinite corpus — SKILL.md conventions, where a skill's checks and tests live, catalog and pack wiring. Use when creating or editing a pack's skills/<name>/ in the canon; a consumer project's own agent docs are authoring-agent-docs' turf.
- writing-tests: Practices for writing tests you can trust. Use before writing or changing any test — see-it-fail discipline, snapshot/golden rules, CI-only and heavy-browser tests, fuzzy-metric gating.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts. - Load before writing any artifact, including Markdown ones — format is part of the design pass, never a speed shortcut.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts — when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, keeping state shared across viewers, handing the viewer a file to save, or updating and republishing itself. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo, defaults to 10m) - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).

First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).

Triggers include: any mention of 'Word doc', 'word document', '.docx', '.dotx', or requests to produce professional documents with formatting like tables of contents, headings, page numbers, or letterheads. description: How to write instruction files coding agents follow reliably. Use before writing or editing any Claude instruction doc — a project CLAUDE.md, a convention doc, a routine spec.

# Writing instruction files coding agents follow

How to author the files an AI coding agent reads — a project CLAUDE.md, a convention doc, an
agent or automation spec — so it follows them reliably. Grounded entirely in Anthropic's
published guidance; bracketed numbers cite the sources listed at the end.

## Know what an instruction file is (and isn't)

- Treat the file as context, not enforced configuration: the agent reads it and tries to
  follow it, with no guarantee of strict compliance. Anything that must happen every time
  (block a write, run a linter before commit) belongs in a deterministic hook instead. [1][2]
- Everything loaded at session start competes for a finite attention budget, and recall
  degrades as context grows ("context rot"). Aim for the smallest set of high-signal tokens
  that produces the behavior you want. [4]
- Keep the always-loaded file to facts that apply broadly in every session. Move multi-step
  procedures and sometimes-relevant domain knowledge into on-demand skills, and rules that
  matter for only part of the codebase into path-scoped rule files. [1][2]

## Decide each line's right to exist

- Include what the agent can't infer from code: build and test commands, style rules that
  differ from language defaults, repo etiquette (branch naming, PR conventions),
  project-specific architecture decisions, required env vars, non-obvious gotchas. [2]
- Exclude what it can figure out by reading code: standard conventions, file-by-file codebase
  descriptions, detailed API docs (link instead), frequently changing facts, and self-evident
  practices like "write clean code". [2]
- For each line, ask: "Would removing this cause the agent to make mistakes?" If not, cut it.
  Bloated instruction files cause the agent to ignore the instructions that matter. [2]
- Target under 200 lines per CLAUDE.md; longer files consume more context and reduce
  adherence. Splitting into imports organizes but does not save context — imports still load
  at launch. [1]

## Write each rule

- Be concrete enough to verify: "Use 2-space indentation", not "Format code properly";
  "Run `npm test` before committing", not "Test your changes". [1]
- Apply the golden rule: show the instruction to a colleague with minimal context — if they'd
  be confused, the agent will be too. [3]
- State the motivation behind a rule, not just the rule; the model generalizes from the
  explanation. [3]
- Tell the agent what to do instead of what not to do: "write flowing prose paragraphs"
  steers better than "do not use markdown". [3]
- Use numbered steps when the order or completeness of steps matters. [3]
- Prefer a few (3–5) diverse, canonical examples over a laundry list of edge-case rules, and
  wrap them in `<example>` tags so they can't be mistaken for instructions. [3][4]
- Pitch rules at the right altitude: specific enough to guide behavior, flexible enough to
  leave the model strong heuristics — avoiding both brittle hardcoded if-then logic and vague
  guidance that assumes shared context. [4]
- Reserve emphasis ("IMPORTANT", "YOU MUST") for tuning adherence on rules that slip. [2]

## Shape a rule so it fires

House practice rather than published guidance — the rest of this file cites its sources, and
this section has none. It is how the rules in this corpus's `RULES.md` files are phrased.

- **Keying a rule to its trigger** — open with the act the reader is performing, not the state
  of the world the rule applies to. Nobody notices that "a value is unknown"; they notice they
  are writing an encoder. A rule keyed to a state never fires, because nothing brings the
  reader to it.
- **Keying a rule the reader reaches while debugging** — name the symptom that sends them
  looking ("A fetch to a host you listed failing in-browser"), not the act that caused it. By
  the time the rule is wanted the act is over, and the symptom is what they can see.
- **Keying a rule that corrects a misconception** — name what the reader wants ("Wanting
  `import`/`export` in extension code"), not the wrong move they might make ("Reaching for a
  bundler"). Someone who doesn't yet know the move is wrong won't recognise themselves in it.
- **Phrasing that trigger** — use the words the reader would use for the situation, and put
  them first and in bold, so the rule is findable by scanning the left margin alone.
- **Choosing the unit** — one block per situation, not one bullet per rule. A reader arrives
  holding a problem, so give them the whole decision in one place rather than a cross-reference
  to three neighbouring bullets.
- **Splitting a rule that only makes sense after the one above it** — don't. If the subject
  needs a "that" pointing back ("Writing that record"), it is a clause of the rule above, not a
  situation of its own. Split when a reader could arrive at the second rule without the first.
- **Ordering a file of many rules** — past roughly fifteen, group them under headings naming the
  surface each concerns, so a reader scans headings before subjects. A flat list that long makes
  every bold subject do the work one heading would.
- **Grouping that separates two rules which qualify each other** — add an explicit pointer from
  the general rule to its exception, or the general one reads as unconditional. That pointer is
  the one sentence a rewrite may add that its source didn't have; name it as an addition when
  you report the change.
- **Ordering the clauses** — the default first, then the `if you can't` fallback, then
  `consider` for an optional aid, then the `don't` that the earlier clauses make unnecessary.
- **Choosing modality** — grade it per clause and claim no more than the rule needs. Keep
  `never` and `always` for the genuinely absolute and reach for `prefer`, `avoid` or `rather
  than` otherwise; escalating a `don't` into a `never` changes the rule rather than rewording
  it.
- **Naming a mechanism** — name the check, helper or skill that owns the mechanics, and stop.
  Its parameters, options and failure modes live with it, and restating them here is a copy
  that goes stale.
- **Closing a block** — say what the other clauses make unnecessary ("don't also comment the
  duplication — the guard covers it"), so nobody adds belt-and-braces.
- **Keeping an exception** — an exception that changes what the reader would do is part of the
  rule; one that only reassures is padding.
- **Cutting a rule's prose** — drop rationale that only restates the rule, examples that
  re-express it, and mechanics another document owns. Keep the motivation itself: a consequence
  the reader needs in order to apply the rule under pressure earns its clause.
- **Rewriting an existing rule** — carry the source's own strength forward. A rewrite must not
  weaken a rule, and it must not strengthen one either.

## Structure the file

- Group related rules under markdown headers and bullets; the agent scans structure the way
  readers do, and organized sections are easier to follow than dense paragraphs. [1]
- Separate content types — background, instructions, tool guidance, output format — into
  distinct sections with consistent, descriptive names (Markdown headers or XML tags). [3][4]
- Make a task spec self-contained: name the files and interfaces involved, state what is out
  of scope, and end with an end-to-end verification step that proves the work. [2]
- Give the agent a check it can run — a test suite, build exit code, linter, or comparison
  script. Without one, "looks done" is its only stopping signal. [2]

## Maintain it like code

- Start minimal and add rules in response to observed failures: the agent makes the same
  mistake a second time, a review catches something it should have known, or you retype last
  session's correction. [1][4]
- Test edits by observing whether behavior actually shifts. If a rule keeps being ignored,
  the file is probably too long and the rule is lost in the noise. [2]
- Remove contradictions: if two rules conflict — including across nested or imported files —
  the agent may pick one arbitrarily. [1]
- Prune regularly. If the agent already behaves correctly without a rule, delete it or
  convert it to a hook. Check the file into version control so the team contributes and it
  compounds in value. [2]
- When a practice is withdrawn, rewrite the docs that taught it into the **current** rule in the
  present tense — never leave a passage narrating what used to be done and why it stopped. A reader
  who never knew the practice doesn't need to be taught it in order to be told the rule, and
  describing a withdrawn technique is how it keeps getting rediscovered; the history belongs to the
  commit that removed it. This bans narrating a *superseded* way of working, not evidence — measured
  costs that argue a live rule is worth its space stay. And retiring a practice is not the moment to
  install a guard against it: a check earns its place from a mistake that repeats, not from the
  deletion that prompted it.

## Sources

- [1] https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory
- [2] https://code.claude.com/docs/en/best-practices
- [3] https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/be-clear-and-direct
- [4] https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/effective-context-engineering-for-ai-agents

1	# Claudinite — the canon's own non-portable working rules
2	
3	This is the Claudinite home repo's own local pack: the capture surface for lessons that are
4	**specific to working on the canon itself** and would not make sense mounted into a consuming
5	project. Portable lessons — anything true for repos beyond this one — belong in the shared canon
6	under `packs/`/`skills/` instead (proposed by PR, or lifted by the promote stage).
7	
8	The growth lifecycle writes here automatically: the `growth-extract` daily task routes the canon's
9	own non-portable lessons — mined from repo activity and from captured conversations alike — into
10	this pack (each at the local promotion ladder's strongest mechanism — a check where the rule is deterministic, otherwise terse
11	prose below).
12	
13	## Standing owner decisions — settled, do not re-litigate
14	
15	- **`canon-curation` lives in `.claudinite/local/packs/`, not `packs/`** (owner decision,
16	  2026-07-19). The canon home's curation duties are Claudinite-maintaining-Claudinite —
17	  project-specific content on the home's own capture surface. Do not propose moving it back, and
18	  do not describe the move as open or provisional.
19	- **Local-pack `run_daily` scheduling is ON — the fleet's default path** (same decision). The
20	  planner reads every member's local-pack daily descriptors by default; never reintroduce an
21	  "experimental / not enabled" framing or an opt-in seam for it.
22	- **Packs-tree segregation is barriers configuration only.** Any rule about what the `packs/`
23	  tree may reference is expressed by declaring/configuring the `barriers` pack (contributed
24	  edges, `siblings`/`scope` capabilities — extend barriers generically if a capability is
25	  missing). Never write standalone code that checks packs-tree segregation.
26	- **A `docs/<initiative>/DESIGN.md` records the mechanism only** (owner decision, 2026-07-23,
27	  #420). Status, phase tracking, in-flight-PR reconciliation and remaining work live in that
28	  initiative's tracking issue (task-prework → #394); a phased plan lives in the sibling
29	  `MIGRATION.md`. Don't reintroduce a status / open-questions / remaining-work section there.
30	- **Multi-session work hands off through the tracking issue, never a prepared prompt** (owner
31	  correction, 2026-07-23). The owner's opener is `continue work on #<n>`, so state not written
32	  into the issue is lost. Before ending a session on unfinished work, update the issue and let
33	  the session summary be a pointer to it — never compose a bespoke "pick up from here" prompt.
34	- **The canon never knows which repos consume it — fleet-wide aggregation is Sheepdog's domain**
35	  (owner correction, 2026-07-28, #520). Designing anything that spans repos, the tempting shape is
36	  a member list (or a "fleet" task) living in the canon. It doesn't go here: the canon carries only
37	  **mechanisms exercised on itself**, and the knowledge of *which* repos exist stays in the
38	  **Sheepdog** repo and its pack, which enumerates members at runtime from its own
39	  `.claudinite-checks.json` entry — exactly where the `fleet-roster` sweep already keeps
40	  it. So a cross-repo feature splits in two: a self-contained per-repo half in the canon, and the
41	  aggregation half as a Sheepdog fleet task. **No repo list exists anywhere in canon code** — and a
42	  derived fleet artifact lands in Sheepdog as a daily **auto-merged PR of a `GENERATED` file**,
43	  never a direct commit to its `main`.
44	- **A pack default stays in the pack — don't ask it at adoption, don't write it into a member's
45	  config** (owner ruling, 2026-07-28, #527/#528). An adoption question whose recommended answer is
46	  right for nearly everyone is "bad noise": it taxes every adopting repo to re-state the default,
47	  and materializing that answer into `.claudinite-checks.json` freezes a copy that then drifts from
48	  the pack and has to be migrated. Keep the default in the pack's own code, ask nothing, and let the
49	  rare project that wants to differ add the setting by hand. Read config as *optional* — an unset
50	  key means "the default", never "misconfigured" (`retention_days` unset is precisely why the
51	  growth-extract retention prune is skipped rather than failing).
52	
53	- **What Claudinite ships must run on the credentials and settings a member already has**
54	  (owner ruling, 2026-08-06). Requiring a member to flip a platform setting, or to provision a wider
55	  credential (a PAT, an app installation, a new secret), is a last resort — not because it is hard,
56	  but because it is per-repo manual work that reliably does not happen: the capability is then
57	  quietly dead in every repo nobody configured, indistinguishable from a Claudinite bug, while the
58	  automation's own report says nothing is wrong. Three members filed issues asking for the same
59	  Actions approval setting (ClaudiniteWebsite#95, EdFringeNow#205, TLDR#182); none was changed, and
60	  each repo's converge kept succeeding while its mount fell a day behind. Prefer the route that
61	  works with the Action's own `GITHUB_TOKEN` and stock configuration even when it is less direct,
62	  and where a platform behaviour blocks you, neutralise its *effect* rather than asking for the
63	  platform to be reconfigured. Where no such route exists — a capability the default credential
64	  cannot hold at all, which is why `FLEET_GITHUB_TOKEN` is legitimate — take the requirement
65	  deliberately: name the exact scope, say why nothing weaker suffices, and have the automation
66	  report when it is missing rather than silently degrading.
67	
68	- **A change to what members receive is not verified until a member has received it — force that in
69	  the same session** (owner requirement, 2026-08-06: *"We're not waiting till tomorrow to see if
70	  something worked"*). Merging to canon is evidence about canon; the only thing that exercises a
71	  canon change end to end is a member's converge, and on a daily slot that is a day away — so a
72	  session that closes on "it reaches the fleet tonight" has shipped an unverified change and hands
73	  the owner a question they will ask anyway (asked five separate ways across 2026-08-05/06:
74	  *"Check status"*, *"Did the Sheepdog baselining work?"*, *"check now"*, *"How do you know 'the
75	  fleet is now fully on 076c029'?"*, and forced baselines appended to three consecutive `lgtm`s).
76	  After landing anything that alters what baselining delivers, drive Sheepdog's `fleet-baseline`
77	  workflow with `follow` and report what it did per member, unasked. Two corollaries. **A dispatch
78	  is not a result** — the API's 204 means queued. And **attaching a member repo to the session is a
79	  read you already have**, so attach the repos the verification needs rather than offering to: *"2
80	  of 11 members confirmed … say the word and I'll attach and verify"* bought a round-trip, one of
81	  four the owner spent that morning telling this session to attach repos.
82	
83	- **A code deprecation rides the standard `@deprecated` tag — never a bespoke conformance check**
84	  (owner ruling, 2026-08-09, #707). Retiring a field, option or module does not earn its own rule
85	  module, test file and catalog row: that is machinery to say what one JSDoc line says, and it grows
86	  once per retirement forever. `deprecated-session-scope` was authored as a `basics` check and deleted
87	  the same day it was reviewed (*"I don't think we want to add a check for every code deprecation"*).
88	  Put `@deprecated` on the **definition** — the one place the thing is declared, here the
89	  `session_scope` section of `engine/scheduler/task-contract.mjs` — and have each sanctioned holdout
90	  pacify the warning with a comment at its own declaration site saying why it still carries the field.
91	  Keep the contract **validating** the lingering field either way: validation catches a typo that would
92	  otherwise strand a dispatch, and is not the same thing as a conformance rule.
93	
94	## Canon-specific gotchas
95	
96	- **Baselining backfill skips the home.** The nightly baselining that lands a `seededByDefault`
97	  pack (and canon-delivered declaration changes) on every member is gated `!isHome`, so the canon
98	  home is the one repo it never reaches: what the fleet receives automatically, this repo's own
99	  `.claudinite-checks.json` only ever gets by hand.
100	- **Pack discovery imports the whole pack tree eagerly — declaration is irrelevant.**
101	  `discoverPacks` imports every `packs/<name>/pack.mjs` on disk and `scanSkillChecks` imports
102	  every `<pack>/skills/<skill>/checks.mjs` beside it, *before* activation is consulted. So
103	  anything in that import graph loads in every repo under every declaration, and a module that is
104	  also a CLI entry point gets re-imported while it is still evaluating: a top-level `await` in its
105	  entry block then never settles and Node exits 13 having run nothing (#581 — `interview.mjs
106	  check` deadlocked fleet-wide, invisible because the SessionStart orchestrator's fail-soft reads
107	  it as a merely-absent note). Start the work *after* evaluation completes — `check(…).catch(…)`.
108	  Enforced by `pack-discovery-entry-await`; the corollary it can't check is to keep these modules
109	  import-light in the first place.
110	- **A pack's `RULES.md` is injected into every session that declares the pack — an idea nobody can
111	  act on belongs in `docs/`, and a pack file must not link there.** Deferred directions, blocked
112	  proposals and status live in `docs/` (e.g. `docs/future-directions.md`) precisely because pack
113	  prose costs context in every consumer session. And the pointer cannot go the other way: `docs/`
114	  is outside the vendor set, so a link from any file under `packs/` resolves to nothing in every
115	  consumer — the `reference-integrity` class that reached `main` unnoticed in #424 (and that
116	  check is work-scoped, so it only sees paths the branch itself deletes). Reference `docs/` from
117	  the issue or PR instead.
118	- **A pack's `RULES.md` carries directives an agent must obey — never a walkthrough of how the
119	  feature works** (owner correction, 2026-08-06: *"Rules are context for any agentic work, not for
120	  random explanations"*). The same injection that makes the prose useful makes description
121	  expensive: a paragraph that only *describes* a mechanism is paid for by every session in every
122	  declaring repo and steers none of them. Shipping the fleet-baseline `follow` half, the rule the
123	  change actually added was one sentence — the two extra PAT read scopes a followed run needs —
124	  and everything around it was a feature tour. Behaviour description goes in the module header and
125	  the pack `README.md`, read by whoever works on that code rather than loaded ambiently; the test
126	  before a paragraph goes in is whether an agent could *act* differently for having read it. Same
127	  instinct as the comment rule `basics` now carries (describe the current state, not the change),
128	  applied where the cost is per session rather than per reader.
129	- **Pick a scheduled task's cadence from how often its signal actually moves.** On a member the
130	  mounted canon changes most nights — baselining converges `.claudinite/shared/` daily — so any
131	  precondition reading `sharedMount` fires nearly every night, spending an opus dispatch per
132	  firing. Where the work isn't latency-sensitive (pruning, dedup), a stale item stays harmlessly
133	  correct, so daily buys noise, not freshness: `growth-dedup` moved to `weekly` in #583 and loses
134	  nothing, because the signals are window-scoped (`sinceIso`) and `windowStart` widens to the
135	  widest due task's period — a weekly run sees all 7 days, batched rather than dropped.
136	- **The home doesn't declare `git-github`, so its skills never mount — never conclude "no such
137	  skill" from `.claude/skills/`.** `mount-skills.mjs` filters on the *literal* declaration
138	  (`isActive(p, { packs: declared })`), not the `requires` closure `check_the_world.mjs` resolves,
139	  and the baselining that would normalize that closure into `.claudinite-checks.json` is the one
140	  thing gated `!isHome` — so `merge-to-main` and `git-github-advanced` are simply absent here.
141	  Read `packs/<pack>/skills/<name>/SKILL.md` out of the tracked tree — the corpus *is* this repo,
142	  and an unmounted skill says nothing about whether its procedure applies. The seeding gap above
143	  is a different one (`git-github` arrives by closure, never `seededByDefault`); catching this
144	  one needs `resolveDeclaredPacks` compared against the literal declaration.
145	- **The same blindness on the member side: a session sees only the packs its repo *declares*, so never
146	  conclude from the mount that no canon pack owns a lesson.** A member's `.claudinite/shared/packs/`
147	  holds its declared set, not the canon — so a pack the repo doesn't declare is simply absent, and the
148	  honest-looking reading ("nothing here covers this") is wrong in the one direction that costs most:
149	  the lesson gets homed in a **new local pack** on the member, duplicating canon territory. Measured
150	  2026-08-09 on EdFringeNow: the client-side data-caching rules that belonged to `static-website` went
151	  into a fresh local pack (whose `ruleRoutingGuidance.belongs` ran 31 words against the 20-word cap, so
152	  the session's own selftest was red), because the repo carries no `site.config` and doesn't declare
153	  the pack — nothing in the session pointed at it. The owner did, by URL: *"That pack does exist … move
154	  the changes into that pack and cleanup the EdFringeNow rules."* Since #728 every mount carries
155	  `packs/directory.GENERATED.md`, the catalog of **every** canon pack — read that, not the mounted
156	  subset, before homing a lesson locally. And when the owning pack's territory is merely too narrow,
157	  **widen its `belongs`** rather than route around it: #727 widened `static-website` by two words,
158	  "shipping" → "shipping and serving", and the rules landed where they belonged. (Portable — a promote
159	  candidate for `grow_with_claudinite/extracting-lessons.md`, whose "route to the pack whose territory
160	  owns it" step assumes that pack is visible from the session.)
161	- **Never re-serialize a repo's JSON config to apply an edit — patch the text.** A round-trip
162	  rewrites what it wasn't asked to: Python's `json.dump` defaults to `ensure_ascii=True` (every
163	  non-ASCII character becomes a `\uXXXX` escape), and indent, key order and the trailing newline
164	  become the serializer's opinion. Nothing fails and tests stay green, so it rides onward. Edit
165	  JSON as anchored text; if you must round-trip, pin every lossy default and read the resulting
166	  diff before committing. (Portable — a promote candidate for `repo-text-sweeps`, where a
167	  `\uXXXX`-in-tracked-JSON check would carry it.)
168	- **A canon session with a consumer repo also in its sources will reach for the *consumer's*
169	  merge skill — merge by the skill of the repo you are merging into.** Canon work is routinely
170	  dual-repo (the canon plus the fleet member being piloted), and both repos ship a merge skill
171	  under different names — the canon's `packs/git-github/skills/merge-to-main/` and, say, GCEC's
172	  local `merge-and-ci`. The consumer's skill wins the match on name/description and is followed
173	  to the letter, so the canon-only steps in *its* recipe are silently skipped — repeatedly, the
174	  **post-merge conversation capture** (`node packs/grow_with_claudinite/capture-log.mjs --issue
175	  <n>`, the "After the merge" section of `merge-to-main`). So: before merging in a dual-repo
176	  session, resolve the merge skill **by target repo**, not by which skill matched first — and
177	  treat capture as part of the merge, not as an optional epilogue.
178	- **Fail-soft SessionStart steps hide their own breakage fleet-wide — test the emitted
179	  output, not the exit code.** Every `engine/pack_loader/` SessionStart step
180	  (`run-pack-session-start.mjs`, `mount-skills.mjs`, `env-requirements.mjs`) wraps its body in
181	  `try { ... } catch {}` so a broken loader never blocks a session. That fail-soft is deliberate,
182	  but it means a runtime fault — a wrong dynamic-import target, a renamed module — exits 0 and
183	  simply emits nothing: no error, no signal. And because the engine is vendored verbatim into
184	  every member, one canon regression silently disables that step across the whole fleet at once.
185	  So a step like this must be guarded by a regression test that runs the real script against a
186	  real corpus and asserts the **positive** effect — the output IS emitted — never merely that
187	  `status === 0` (which fail-soft makes meaningless); see
188	  `engine-tests/pack_loader/run-pack-session-start.test.mjs`.
189	- **The nightly self-refresh cannot repair the vendor-set computation — pin operational
190	  files against the REAL canon tree.** Baselining's converge re-runs
191	  `vendoring/compute-vendor-set.mjs` from canon HEAD, so a bug *in that computation* is
192	  the one class of canon regression that is not self-healing: every refresh faithfully
193	  reproduces it, and recovery is an out-of-band vendor refresh applied to each member by
194	  hand. So when the vendor set excludes by *pattern*, an operational file that matches
195	  needs a by-path whitelist (`VENDORED_ENGINE_DOCS`) **and** a regression test asserting
196	  against the real canon tree, not only a synthetic fixture: a fixture keeps proving the
197	  whitelist mechanism works while the live path silently drops out from under it (see the
198	  paired tests in `vendoring/compute-vendor-set.test.mjs`).
199	- **A check that selects its inputs by path pattern can reach zero files and still pass — assert
200	  the live in-scope count.** When skills moved inside their owning pack (#385),
201	  `skill-no-enforcement-narration` kept scanning the root-level `skills/<name>/SKILL.md` layout: it
202	  matched nothing in any tree, read as live, and caught nothing until a human noticed the prose it
203	  should have flagged (#560 — 21 skills in scope once repointed). Its fixtures are why it hid so
204	  well; they spelled the same dead layout, so five green tests proved the *matching* and never the
205	  *selection*. A scan-based check therefore needs one assertion over the **real** tree that its
206	  scope is non-empty. Other half of the same class: agent-facing text pointing where the code isn't
207	  — the same PR fixed a rule whose `why`, fix text and `doc` all named `engine/checks_helpers` or
208	  `checks/lib`, neither of which ever existed. Nothing catches that on its own —
209	  `reference-integrity` is work-scoped and flags only paths the branch itself deletes — so grep the
210	  tree for any directory you name in a finding, a remedy, or a doc pointer before shipping it.
211	- **A scheduled task's precondition gates on movement in the window, never on standing state.** "An
212	  open PR exists" is true forever once it is true once, so the task wakes every night, spends an
213	  agent, and re-derives yesterday's verdict over an unchanged set (three of tidy-repo's tasks
214	  shipped that way; fixed in #554). Gate on the objects' own movement — a `touched` list or a
215	  tip-commit date, which the signal collector has to actually carry (`branches` carried names only,
216	  so "is any of this new" had no answer at all). A signal that is true most days on an active repo
217	  — a substantive `main` move — may only **widen** an already-triggered run, never wake one. And the
218	  gate is not the scope: where a verdict is relative to the rest of the set (superseded-by,
219	  already-in-`main`), newness gates and the full set stays the scope. (Portable — a promote
220	  candidate for `core/scheduled-tasks.md`, which states the precondition contract but not this.)
221	- **You cannot force a due slot by running the scheduler workflow by hand.** Dueness is
222	  stateless — a slot is due iff its time falls in `(last successful run, now]` — so a
223	  `workflow_dispatch` run outside the slot's window succeeds, prints `- no tasks due`, and
224	  does nothing. It looks like a healthy run. To exercise a task Action-side, invoke its
225	  worker directly, or move the slot hour in `taskScheduler` and wait for the cron.
226	- **A scheduled task is gated twice — prove a change through `planRun`, never through its own
227	  precondition.** `planRun` computes the due list *before* any precondition runs, so a task whose
228	  most-recent slot has already been run is never evaluated and never reads its signals at all. #513's
229	  forced-run override landed with every test driving the precondition (or the signal collector) directly
230	  and was inert on exactly the run it existed for — the mid-day manual trigger — because the due-list
231	  gate it never touched had already dropped the task (`evaluations: []`; fixed in #516). A test that
232	  starts *inside* the gate proves only "works once evaluated" and says nothing about whether the task
233	  ever gets there. Drive the real `planRun` from a deliberately **non-due** slot: that is the only shape
234	  that catches it.
235	- **Every due task in a run shares ONE checkout — an agentless worker must not touch it.** The
236	  scheduler runs the whole due list in a single working tree, so a worker that checks out a branch or
237	  leaves an index behind hands the next task a tree it did not expect, and a run that dies leaves the
238	  mess for whatever follows. A task whose output is a regenerated file lands it through
239	  `engine/scheduler/deliver-generated.mjs` — git plumbing against the fetched base tip, with HEAD, the
240	  index and the working tree untouched — and reads its prior state from that base rather than local
241	  HEAD, so stacked runs stay idempotent. (`basics/baselining`'s own deliver is the deliberate
242	  exception: it commits a whole working tree and re-cuts a dated family branch; the landing itself —
243	  delivery preference, CI dispatch, arm/land/merge — is shared, in `engine/scheduler/land-pr.mjs`.)
244	- **A code-search hit is evidence; a code-search miss is not — survey by reading each file.**
245	- **Derive the test file list from the tree — every hand-written glob here under-runs the suite.**
246	  There is no `package.json` and no test script, so each session invents its own incantation and
247	  silently verifies less than it thinks. Measured in this checkout: `node --test <dir>` does not
248	  recurse — it resolves the path as a module and dies with `Cannot find module`; bash `**` is not
249	  recursive without `globstar`, so `engine-tests/**/*.test.mjs packs-tests/**/*.test.mjs` reaches
250	  **37 of 65** tracked test files. Four consecutive sessions (2026-07-26, #459/#452/#435/#468) each
251	  wrote a different command and reported 587, 690, 621 and 697 tests — three of them pushed after
252	  running a strict subset. Neither published list is authoritative either: `ci.yml`'s `tests=(…)`
253	  array omits `vendoring/*.test.mjs`, and `engine/checks/README.md`'s "as CI runs it" one-liner
254	  names `engine/test/`, `skills/` and `mount/`, none of which exist. So enumerate from git and let
255	  the count speak: `node --test $(git ls-files '*.test.mjs')`. (The drift-guard, once the array is
256	  clean: assert every tracked `*.test.mjs` is matched by `ci.yml`'s globs.)
257	- **A branch that waited overnight has lost its base *and* possibly its premise — re-verify the
258	  problem still exists on current `main`, unasked.** This repo merges its own scheduled-task PRs
259	  without a human, on top of multi-phase migrations that retire whole directories: measured on
260	  PR #465, `main` moved **14 commits in 13.7 hours** and one of them (#473, "retire `run_daily/`")
261	  *deleted the file the PR's diagnosis rested on* and had already landed most of its content. The
262	  branch rebased cleanly and the tests stayed green — the change was simply no longer the change to
263	  make, and the correct move was `git checkout -B <branch> origin/main` and re-applying only the
264	  surviving slice (9 files → 2). So syncing the base is not the check; the check is a **content**
265	  one: after `git fetch`, read what the new commits did to the surface you are changing and state
266	  whether the problem is still there, what the goal was, and what survives. Do this whenever you
267	  return to a paused branch, before presenting it — the owner should never have to ask "is this
268	  change still needed" (asked three times on #465 before it was volunteered).
269	- **Re-basing your edit onto a moved `main` means re-applying it, never restoring a whole-file copy.**
270	  A pack's `RULES.md` is append-only and several auto-merged runs write it a day, so a `cp` of the
271	  version you read back over the fetched one deletes their lessons — and nothing goes red, because no
272	  test or check reads prose (caught by luck on 2026-08-11/#758, 54 lines already staged). Re-read the
273	  fetched file, apply the same anchored edit to it, and confirm the stat shows insertions only.
274	- **Every `Claude_Code_Remote` call costs minutes, and a call that returns nothing has NOT failed —
275	  never re-issue it.** The whole server behaves this way, not one tool: measured over four sessions
276	  on 2026-07-29, `add_repo` ran 270–285s a call, `send_later` 117–390s, `list_triggers` 139–325s,
277	  `delete_trigger` 286–301s, `subscribe_pr_activity` 14–237s. They read like cheap registrations,
278	  so a session issues one, sits through minutes of silence, concludes it hung, and issues it again —
279	  and *the duplicate is the dominant cost*, because the first call had already succeeded:
280	  **#562 (`2026-07-29T1500Z`) — 6 `add_repo` calls, 1121s of that session's 1391s of tool
281	  wall-clock (81%)**, with `HelloWorldFlutterApp` added twice (285s + 271s); **#553
282	  (`2026-07-29T2206Z`) — the same PR check-in `send_later`d 4 times, 1107s of 2028s (55%)**; **#544
283	  (`2026-07-29T1248Z`) — `list_triggers` ×2, `delete_trigger` ×2 on one trigger id, `send_later` ×2:
284	  1854s of 2472s (75%)**, in a session whose real work was 166 tool calls. `AskUserQuestion` shares
285	  the shape — #559's session asked one question twice for 218s + 204s. So: **one call per intent,
286	  ever**, and when what you want is "is it green yet", read the check status directly and merge on
287	  the already-green result rather than buying a notification. Budget these calls before making them:
288	  four of them is most of an hour. And to *read* a public sibling repo, `add_repo` is not the route at
289	  all: it attaches nothing and answers that the session's git proxy already serves anonymous reads —
290	  measured 2026-08-11 (#641), 3m40s before the owner interrupted it plus 40s on the re-issue, against

578	  with no action points reads, correctly, as the work not having been done.
579	- **A retry across a call whose outcome you cannot observe needs no arbitration protocol at all —
580	  decline to retry and let an existing sweep close the gap.** The work-item queue's first invocation
581	  design treated the dispatch API as at-least-once and built an agent-side claim/lease specifically to
582	  arbitrate the duplicate a client-side timeout retry could produce. Owner correction (#854, commit
583	  `f0e18dc`, 2026-08-15): *"the API should be called once per item... a retry is only safe when you know
584	  the first call did nothing, and the timeout is exactly the case where you cannot."* Declining to retry
585	  made invocation at-most-once, and the claim/lease had nothing left to collapse — its outcomes reduced
586	  to "refused" (definite, converge to needs-human) and "unanswered" (the item stays with the agent; an
587	  already-existing janitor rule, the agent leash, sweeps the case where no session ever started). Before
588	  building dedup or arbitration machinery around an uncertain call outcome, check whether declining to
589	  retry removes the uncertainty instead of managing it.
590	- **A function meant to be safe to call repeatedly over an object's own lifecycle needs a round-trip
591	  test, not a per-call one.** `withSection` appended a same-named section instead of replacing it in
592	  place, so a work-item body that was written twice — once at birth, once at hand-off — carried two
593	  `### Context` sections, while `instructions.md` reads "the issue's Context section", singular: whichever
594	  section a session read first, the other's content silently vanished (#881, commit `d9509ea`,
595	  2026-08-15). Every existing unit test of `withSection` passed, because each called it once — and
596	  `rollBody` had already hand-stripped its own section before calling `withSection` at one of its two
597	  call sites, a workaround for the same bug nobody had generalized. Where a helper is meant to be
598	  reapplied across a hand-off, a re-queue, or a retry, write a test that calls it twice and asserts no
599	  duplication; a suite of single-call tests can stay green while the multi-call case silently corrupts
600	  state.
601	- **A check's `fix` text carries force independent of its declared `severity` — never write a
602	  config-acceptance escape into an advisory check's remedy.** `basics/file-placement` was
603	  `severity: 'advisory'` and never failed a run, but its `fix` text read *"or accept it in
604	  `.claudinite-checks.json` with a reason if it is a deliberate cross-cutting concern"* — sessions
605	  followed the words, not the severity field, and this repo alone accumulated eight acceptance entries,
606	  each a paragraph, for findings that were never blocking anything. Owner (#856, 2026-08-15): *"That is
607	  cost with no purchase. An acceptance entry exists to make a blocking violation reviewable; on an
608	  advisory finding it buys nothing and taxes every repo that hits the smell."* Fixed in #858 by dropping
609	  the acceptance suggestion and deleting all nine entries. When authoring a check's `fix` line, the
610	  remedies it names must match the severity actually enforced — an advisory finding's only remedies are
611	  act on it or leave it, never a config escape that implies a gate nothing enforces.
612	- **After an `AskUserQuestion` is declined or interrupted, don't re-post the identical question on
613	  resume — take the tool's own recommended default and state the assumption, or open the question up.**
614	  Measured on the #801 session (2026-08-15): the canon-flip endpoint question was asked, declined
615	  (4m40s), re-asked verbatim on resume, declined again (4m36s), then asked a third time before landing —
616	  on the tool's own "Recommended" option (1m33s). The "B6 route" question was asked, declined (4m07s),
617	  re-asked verbatim, declined again (14m00s) — and was never answered by either offered option at all;
618	  the owner instead typed past the popup, in plain prose, "B6 seems not crucial for now. You can continue
619	  without it." Both round-trips cost real minutes to a second identical popup that, in neither case, was
620	  what actually resolved things — the resolution was either the tool's own default or an answer outside
621	  the choice set. A decline is signal that the closed choice set is wrong, not that the same choices need
622	  asking again.
